items.title: Tolliver interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2021
items.q: You know I mean Duke Ellington, you name it.

ctx.x: Did your composing develop as your trumpet playing developed? Let me re-phrase. Do you remember the first time, the first period that you felt I can compose also. I can offer something that can be a tune.

Yes. You know all of our original greats who created this, the realization is is that they are actually composing as they are soloing and it’s inextricably tied together, you know, soloing and composing. So you know, by example, Charlie Parker, all of his compositions are solos set down, scripted later, that became part of the underpinnings compositionally of this art form. Thelonious Monk etcetera. You know I mean Duke Ellington, you name it. And I think somewhere after I came back home from college I actually…
in New York and of course the rest is history with that one with us as well. And it was those chords which, you know, open up compositional vistas for me, and arranging and orchestration and so on.

items.title: Charles Tolliver interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 6, 2021 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Are you speaking of people like Charles Mingus and Ellington?

ctx.x: Well I might have been referring to how I have observed, you know, those few instances when a musician may have, by the way — not by what they say but by the way they perform when they’re playing with you that their minds and persona is not as a team player. You know. And in that case it would be better for them to do their own thing or go do it somewhere else. But generally — it really depends on the flavor and what is the aspirations of anyone that calls you for a gig or what you want to have happen, you know,…
Are you speaking of people like Charles Mingus and Ellington?

Oh absolutely. Absolutely. But also Max Roach and Clifford Brown. They created a repertory that will live forever, a repertory of using the Great American Songbook, as well as their own compositions, and putting arrangements to them that will last forever. I mean the show — Broadway writers had no idea that those beautiful songs that they wrote that became a part of the American Songbook could be completely made even better you know, with chord substitutions and rhythmical arrangements and rhythmical
